summary.text: Micas are a group of silicate minerals whose crystals split easily into thin, fragile, elastic plates.
This perfect basal cleavage comes from their structure: stacked layers held to each other only by weak ionic bonds.
Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rock and goes into drywall, paints and electronics, and into cosmetics and food for shimmer.

facts.label: Largest documented crystal
facts.value: About 330 tonnes, from Lacey Mine, Ontario

items.prompt: You can peel a mica crystal apart with a fingernail into thin, bendy sheets. Why does it come apart so neatly?

options.label: Its layers are only weakly bonded together
Water inside it freezes and pries it open
It is many separate flakes glued together
Its atoms have no regular arrangement

items.explain: Mica is built of layers joined by relatively weak ionic bonds, which gives it perfect basal cleavage.

items.prompt: Why is ground mica added to some cosmetics and foods?
items.explain: Mica is used in cosmetics and food to add "shimmer" or "frost".

items.prompt: A company wants large mica crystals it can cut into sheets. Where should it look first?
items.explain: Large mica crystals are typically mined from granitic pegmatites, the most important source of sheet mica.

items.prompt: Mica is sold as large sheets or as small flakes and scrap. Which form is far less abundant?
items.explain: Sheet mica is considerably less abundant than flake and scrap mica, and the best grades sell for far more.

items.prompt: Two micas, one white and one black, are found side by side. What mainly sets them apart?
items.explain: All micas crystallize in the same system with similar structures; they vary in chemical composition and colour.

items.prompt: Mica is common in two of the three main rock families but turns up only occasionally, as small flakes, in the third. Which one?

options.label: None; it is equally common in all

items.explain: Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rock and only occasionally found as small flakes in sedimentary rock.
